text:
Recent work supports history perturbations as diagnostics of model dependence. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) reports that excessive emphasis on recent interactions can hurt recommendation accuracy. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) uses shuffling to reveal weak sequential structure in several popular datasets; [Liu et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that temporal signals can reflect item availability as well as user behavior. [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history edits that change recommendations, providing a direct precedent for paired sensitivity probes.

Repetition and saturation require separate interpretation. [Repetition and Exploration (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3539618.3591914) identifies repetition shortcuts and bias associated with shared item embeddings. [Learning to Forget (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12714) models post-purchase satiation through temporal suppression and replenishment signals. Its purchase-aware assumptions cannot be inferred from generic interaction histories: repeated semantic interests need not mean repeat-item consumption, and observed interactions do not establish fulfilled needs.

Suggested adaptation: evaluate fixed training-history prefixes against paired recent-only truncation, recent-suffix removal, deletion of repeated-interest evidence, deletion of isolated old interactions, and order shuffling. Define semantic groups using available titles/descriptions; match deletion counts and age distributions, preserve candidate sets, and distinguish position-preserving masking from sequence compaction. Measure candidate score/rank changes and top-10 overlap alongside encoder-feature changes; compare full shuffling with last-item-fixed shuffling to isolate final-event dependence. These are proposed diagnostics, not established intent measurements: sensitivity reveals dependence on supplied evidence, while saturation and temporal shortcut explanations remain hypotheses. Keep benchmark splits and the macro validation HR@10 selection rule unchanged.
